Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=12,$ located in the second quadrant, shown above?

activity_context.topic_title: Line Integrals of Scalar Functions Over Ellipses

examples.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Ellipse
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/71df4fc7bd52fe5dd97c7e01502dec2ad68ae31fdf224cccd812c6b7318c70b7.png)

Find, as a definite integral, an expression for the line integral of the function $\displaystyle\int_\limits{C} 2xy \:\textrm{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the right half of the ellipse $9x^2 + 4y^2 = 36,$ shown above.
examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 3\sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 2xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}3y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $49{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{7}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $7,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,7\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+49{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=21\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}3y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }21\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =21{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
